top_choice_rationale: P001 (Autor, Hanson, Katz) answers a first-order causal question, who gains and loses when technology and trade shift labour demand. It pairs a conceptual account of skill demand and supply with transparent local-labour-market designs. A decade or more of replication and critique has refined magnitudes and persistence but has not overturned the finding that adjustment is slow, geographically concentrated and costly. I would word the citation around labour demand, wages and local labour markets, not around the task model as theory. That avoids claiming priority over Acemoglu, Levy and Murnane and limits overlap with the 2023 and 2024 prizes. The main cost is Dorn's exclusion under the three-name cap, plus the risk that the citation reads as two strands joined by Autor. That is a question of citation scope, not merit. P002 (Kiyotaki and Moore) has cleaner attribution and is mature, and I rank it second. Its quantitative importance is established more indirectly and it is partly adjacent to the 2022 prize, so its confirmation is thinner than P001's. Both awards are scientifically defensible, so no award (P000) ranks last. I do not treat the number of members supporting P001 as evidence of merit.
recusal_note: None apparent from profile: no co-authorship or institutional tie to Autor, Hanson, Katz, Kiyotaki or Moore. Disclosed adjacency only: I am a political scientist whose work on the political consequences of economic dislocation draws on the B027 literature. I am a Stockholm University colleague, in a different department, of Hassler, Krusell and Boppart. These ties are disclosed, not adjudicated.
